results.result: The authors established multipatch setups with 10 Sensapex and 8 Scientifica manipulators using custom-made stages with optimized geometry (27° approach angle, aluminum/steel construction) and integrated hardware for simultaneous 10-channel recording.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 describe the physical setup with specific technical details (manipulator types, stage materials, approach angles, amplifier configuration) that are documented in methods and shown in Figure 1. The technical specifications are concrete and verifiable.

results.result: An automated pressure control system was developed that can be built within one week with basic equipment, uses multiple pressure levels (20 mbar LOW, 70 mbar HIGH), and is applicable to any patch-clamp setup to reduce errors and increase experimental speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 and C72-C76 describe the pressure system with specific technical parameters and benefits. The system is documented in Figure 2 with detailed schematics. While the claimed benefits (C76) are somewhat speculative, the core technical achievement is well-documented.

results.result: Pipette cleaning using Alconox solution enables immediate reuse with >10 successful repatches. In rat pyramidal neurons (n=67), no systematic changes in cellular or synaptic properties were detected after cleaning (p>0.05, mean relative differences 0-10%), validating the cleaning protocol.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 present quantitative validation data from 67 rat neurons with appropriate statistical testing (repeated measures ANOVA, p>0.05) shown in Figure 3I-L. The validation is thorough, though the authors appropriately note limitations and recommend user-specific validation (methods text).

results.result: Performance benchmarking across 6-, 8-, and 10-pipette configurations showed declining success rates (88±12%, 85±13%, 79±11%) and increasing experimental times (36.6±2.3 min to 46.1±4.6 min) as pipette numbers increased, with tested connections scaling from 23±7 to 56±17.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 present systematic performance data with sample sizes (n=30, 33, 10) and quantitative metrics shown in Figure 4B-D. The declining success rate with increased pipette numbers is well-documented and supports the conclusion (C88) that conventional scaling becomes impractical.

results.result: The clean-to-complete strategy increased average cluster sizes to 7.8±0.4 (97±5% success rate, n=16) for 8 pipettes and 9.2±0.6 (92±6% success rate, n=9) for 10 pipettes by enabling immediate cleaning and reuse of failed pipettes during experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 presents quantitative improvements with sample sizes shown in Figure 5B-C. The success rates represent substantial improvements over conventional approaches (C39-C42), demonstrating the practical benefit of the cleaning system.

results.result: The clean-to-extend strategy increased tested connections from 140±24 to 244±52 per animal (n=6) on the 8-pipette setup. Distance distributions remained similar across recording rounds (median 84-85 μm), indicating no systematic spatial bias.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 presents quantitative data with sample size shown in Figure 5D-E. Claim C94 addresses potential spatial bias with distance analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), strengthening the conclusion that sequential patching doesn't introduce systematic artifacts.

results.result: Using two rounds of clean-to-extend, up to 17 neighboring neurons were recorded in one human slice, with two neurons maintained across all sessions to probe complex connectivity patterns including their connections to 16 other neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C98 describe a specific experimental demonstration shown in Figure 6A-D. The connectivity matrix clearly shows the 17 neurons and detected connections, providing direct visual evidence for the claimed capability.

results.result: Using two setups simultaneously, 300-700 potential synaptic connections were probed from individual human patients within 24 hours (up to 99 neurons recorded), generating sample sizes comparable to previous studies that pooled multiple subjects.
results.evaluation: Claims C47 and C22 present the throughput achievement shown in Figure 6E-F with data from three patients (336-694 tested connections). Claim C99 contextualizes this with citations to previous pooled studies, demonstrating the advance in per-patient data yield.

results.result: Excitatory connectivity between pyramidal cells in human cortical layer 2/3 ranged from 12.9-17.7% across three patients, similar to previous reports. Inter-individual differences were not statistically different (p>0.05) but were statistically equivalent within ±5-9.5%.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 present connectivity measurements with appropriate statistical testing (Fisher's exact test, equivalence testing with 90% CI) shown in Figure 6G. The comparison to previous studies (C100) with citations validates the measurements and demonstrates consistency.

results.result: Optimizations including a prefill device and semi-automated pipette positioning reduced preparation times to 11-13 minutes for filling/mounting and 7-9 minutes for positioning, as shown in Figure 4C.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 present specific time measurements shown in Figure 4C. These are straightforward timing measurements that support the efficiency improvements, though they represent incremental optimizations rather than major innovations.

results.result: The semi-automated approach achieved higher success rates (88%/85%/79%) than fully automated systems (43-51%) and faster positioning (53-55 s/pipette vs 103 s), though manual patching took slightly longer (126-154 s vs 120 s), leading to the conclusion that full automation would require disproportionate effort.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 compare performance to published automated systems with specific citations (Wu et al., 2016; Kolb et al., 2019). The comparison is quantitative and supports the authors' assessment (C128) that their hybrid approach represents a practical optimum, though this conclusion involves some subjective judgment.

results.result: The combined improvements represent a substantial increase in experimental output compared to previous studies requiring data pooling across subjects, enabling microcircuit analysis at the individual patient level and potentially reducing animal numbers needed for statistically significant findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 and C143 synthesize the overall impact with appropriate citations (Seeman et al., 2018; Thomson and Lamy, 2007). The conclusion is well-supported by the demonstrated throughput (C47, C99) and validated measurements (C48-C49), representing the main contribution of the work.

results.result: The authors discuss that underestimation of synaptic connectivity in slice experiments is an ongoing concern, with correction factors ranging from 1.1-1.7 depending on the source of error (axon cutting vs detection limits), and recommend avoiding superficial cells and controlling for distance and recording quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C119 present a balanced discussion of methodological limitations with appropriate citations to the relevant literature. This represents a thoughtful consideration of potential systematic errors rather than a novel finding, appropriately placed in the discussion.

results.result: The authors compare multipatch to alternative methods (all-optical approaches, calcium/voltage imaging, optogenetic stimulation), noting that while these can probe more neurons (20-200), multipatch provides superior access to cellular/synaptic properties, doesn't require genetic modification, and is uniquely suited for measuring synaptic strength and plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C142 provide a comprehensive comparison to alternative methods with appropriate citations throughout. This represents a fair assessment of the trade-offs between methods, appropriately acknowledging both advantages and limitations of the multipatch approach.

results.result: The authors validated their pipette cleaning protocol by comparing cellular and synaptic properties of neurons recorded before and after cleaning in both rat and human tissue. They found no systematic changes in properties like resting membrane potential, input resistance, spontaneous EPSP frequency/amplitude, and action potential kinetics after up to two cleaning cycles, with mean relative differences between 0-10% and p>0.05 for all comparisons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised a major concern (Essential revision #1) that the authors 'omitted' the aCSF rinsing step from the original Forest protocol and provided 'little or no data' to support this practice. They specifically requested data on 'how the membrane potential, input resistance, synaptic events, and action potential parameters change over time after patching and repatching.' While the authors provided extensive validation data in rat tissue (C36-C38, C167) and some human tissue comparisons (C168-C174), the reviewers' concern about the omitted rinsing step and request for temporal dynamics suggests the validation was incomplete or not fully convincing in the initial submission.

results.result: The authors developed multipatch setups with 6, 8, and 10 manipulators, achieving success rates of 88±12%, 85±13%, and 79±11% respectively, with corresponding average tested connections of 23±7, 41±13, and 56±17. They implemented semi-automated pipette positioning and prefilling approaches to reduce experimental time, though success rates decreased and experimental time increased (from 36.6±2.3 to 46.1±4.6 min) as the number of pipettes increased.
results.evaluation: The reviewers acknowledged the methodology was 'well laid out, with appropriate drawings, photos, parts lists, and videos' and should be 'an accessible method.' The acceptance summary explicitly states the authors 'show their robotic system can obtain high numbers of successful paired recordings.' No specific concerns were raised about the performance metrics or setup configurations, indicating reviewer acceptance of these technical achievements.

results.result: The clean-to-complete strategy increased average cluster size on 8- and 10-pipette setups to 7.8±0.4 (97±5% success rate) and 9.2±0.6 (92±6% success rate) respectively. Pipettes from failed recording attempts could be immediately cleaned and reused, even simultaneously with ongoing patch attempts, greatly increasing the success rate and yield of experiments.
results.evaluation: The acceptance summary explicitly states the system 'can obtain high numbers of successful paired recordings in part due to a system that allows for cleaning and reusing patch electrodes for multiple serial recordings.' The reviewers acknowledged this as a key innovation and did not raise concerns about the clean-to-complete performance metrics, indicating acceptance of these results.

results.result: Using both cleaning strategies (clean-to-complete and clean-to-extend), the authors increased tested connections from 140±24 to 244±52 per animal in rodent experiments. In human tissue, they recorded up to 17 neighboring neurons in one slice and up to 99 neurons probing 300-700 connections from individual patients within 24 hours. The distance distribution remained similar across sequential recording rounds, and the approach could unveil complex connectivity patterns beyond simple pairwise statistics.
results.evaluation: The acceptance summary states the approach 'yields hundreds of potential neural pairs per patient sample, which will undoubtedly yield novel insights.' Reviewers requested clarification on experimental details (Essential revision #3) including 'the time that is taken to probe connectivity and an analysis of the distance distribution,' which the authors appear to have addressed (C94). The overall throughput achievements were accepted as demonstrated.

results.result: The method enabled probing of 150 synaptic connections between 17 neurons in one human slice and screening of over 600 connections from single patients. Excitatory connectivity between pyramidal cells in human layer 2/3 ranged from 12.9-17.7%, similar to previous reports, with inter-individual differences not statistically different from each other. Sample sizes from single patients were comparable to datasets generated by pooling multiple subjects, representing a substantial increase in performance.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the high throughput, they raised concerns about connectivity analysis. Essential revision #2 states 'The article overemphasizes connectivity analysis and ignores its limitations, e.g., false negatives' and suggests emphasizing that multipatch is 'currently the only technique available to assay the strength and short-term plasticity of monosynaptic connectivity.' Essential revision #5 questions whether the data will be 'sufficient yet to probe the difference between individuals' and suggests the authors 'tone down this claim.' This indicates reviewer uncertainty about the connectivity findings and their interpretation.

results.result: The authors developed an automated pressure system that can be built within a week with basic equipment, using specific pressure settings (20 mbar LOW, 70 mbar HIGH) for different experimental phases. The system is applicable to any patch-clamp setup and can reduce experimental errors, increase speed, and help experimenters concentrate on essential tasks.
results.evaluation: The acceptance summary explicitly mentions 'automated pressure control' as one of the 'recent innovations' the authors 'adopted and optimized.' The reviewers stated the methodology was 'well laid out' and should be accessible, with no specific concerns raised about the pressure system design or implementation.

results.result: The semi-automated approach achieved higher success rates (88%/85%/79%) compared to fully automated systems (43-51%) and was faster for pipette positioning (53/55 s vs 103 s per pipette), though slightly slower for approaching cells and establishing whole-cell configuration (126/154 s vs 120 s). The authors concluded that fully automated multipatch would require disproportionate effort and that slice exchange and cell selection would still require human presence.
results.evaluation: The acceptance summary describes the method as 'semi-automated' and reviewers acknowledged the 'benefits of the semi-automated approach' (Essential revision #4). The comparison with fully automated systems and the rationale for the semi-automated design were not challenged, indicating reviewer acceptance of this approach and its performance advantages.

results.result: Automated data analysis is an essential step to leverage the increased experimental throughput. A previous study demonstrated an automatic synapse detection algorithm using a support vector machine classifier that achieved 95% accuracy.
results.evaluation: Essential revision #4 states that authors 'do not identify other aspects of multipatch experiments that could benefit from automation – for example, data acquisition and online QC, and real-time connection detection.' The reviewers also noted that 'With the potential for so much data gathering, data format (e.g. Neurodata without borders), data sharing, automation of connection detection and analysis, should be addressed.' This indicates the reviewers felt these aspects were insufficiently addressed in the original submission.

results.result: The authors discussed limitations of slice experiments including underestimation of synaptic connectivity due to axon cutting, with correction factors ranging from 1.1-1.7 reported in different studies. They noted that in vivo recordings found 6.7% connection probability compared to 9.3% in slices, and emphasized the importance of avoiding superficial cells, controlling for intersomatic distances, and ensuring good recording quality.
results.evaluation: Essential revision #2 explicitly requested that authors address connectivity analysis limitations, stating 'The article overemphasizes connectivity analysis and ignores its limitations, e.g., false negatives.' The inclusion of this extensive discussion of limitations and methodological considerations (C113-C119) appears to address this concern, and the acceptance summary indicates the overall approach was validated, suggesting these limitations were adequately discussed in revision.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on pressure system (C28-C30, C72-C76). Both evaluations find the automated pressure control well-documented and supported. OpenEval notes some speculation about benefits (C76), while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as an adopted innovation with no concerns raised.

Perfect agreement on electrode cleaning system performance (C44, C78-C79, C92). Both evaluations support the quantitative improvements and acknowledge this as a key innovation enabling high-throughput serial recordings.

Perfect agreement on semi-automated approach comparison (C125-C129). Both evaluations accept the comparison with fully automated systems and the rationale for the hybrid design as a practical optimum.

Perfect agreement on methodological limitations discussion (C113-C119). Both evaluations support the balanced treatment of connectivity analysis limitations, with peer reviewers explicitly requesting this discussion in Essential revision #2.

Disagreement on validation sufficiency (C31-C38). OpenEval finds the quantitative validation thorough and supported with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers raised major concerns (Essential revision #1) about omitted aCSF rinsing and requested additional temporal dynamics data, rating this UNCERTAIN.

Agreement on physical setup documentation (C23-C27). OpenEval finds technical specifications concrete and verifiable. Peer reviewers acknowledge methodology was 'well laid out' with appropriate documentation, indicating acceptance of setup claims.

Agreement on conventional performance metrics (C39-C43, C84, C87). OpenEval finds systematic performance data well-documented. Peer reviewers acknowledged the system 'can obtain high numbers of successful paired recordings' with no specific concerns about these baseline measurements.

Agreement on timing measurements (C81-C82). OpenEval finds these straightforward measurements supporting efficiency improvements. Peer reviewers accepted the methodology as 'well laid out' with no concerns about timing data.

Agreement on experimental demonstration (C46, C97-C98). OpenEval finds the 17-neuron connectivity demonstration well-documented. Peer reviewers accepted the throughput achievements, though requested clarification on experimental details including distance distribution (C94).

Agreement on sequential patching data (C45, C94). OpenEval finds quantitative data and spatial bias analysis support the conclusions. Peer reviewers requested distance distribution analysis, which appears to have been addressed in C94.

Disagreement on connectivity measurements (C48-C49, C100). OpenEval finds statistical testing appropriate and measurements validated. Peer reviewers raised concerns (Essential revisions #2, #5) about overemphasis on connectivity analysis, false negatives, and whether data is sufficient to probe individual differences, rating this UNCERTAIN.

Partial disagreement on throughput claims (C22, C47, C99). OpenEval supports the throughput achievement and contextualization. Peer reviewers acknowledged high throughput but questioned interpretation (Essential revision #5), suggesting authors 'tone down' claims about probing individual differences.

Partial overlap on overall impact (C101-C103, C143). OpenEval finds the synthesis well-supported by demonstrated results. Peer reviewers acknowledged the approach 'will undoubtedly yield novel insights' but raised concerns about connectivity analysis limitations and interpretation.

OpenEval evaluated comprehensive comparison to alternative methods (C132-C142) as SUPPORTED with fair assessment of trade-offs. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these comparative claims.

Peer reviewers raised concerns (Essential revision #4) about insufficient discussion of automation opportunities in data acquisition, QC, connection detection, and data sharing/format (C130-C131), rating this UNCERTAIN. No corresponding OpenEval result found addressing these future automation aspects.
